text:
#Allergic #rhinitis and #chronic #rhinosinusitis are common, frequently coexisting upper airway inflammatory diseases linked by shared type 2 immune mechanisms. However, broad variations in sensitisation patterns and treatment response obscure optimal surgical and pharmacological dosing. Advancing care relies on integrating prospective real-world data, non-invasive biomarkers, and personalized treatment.

In this issue, Lundberg and van Waterschoot et al. review surgical options for refractory non-allergic rhinitis in an EAACI Task Force position paper, from inferior turbinate reduction to posterior nasal nerve ablation. Sousa-Pinto et al. use a dose-response network meta-analysis to show that doubling the dose of intranasal medications outperforms adding oral antihistamines in allergic rhinitis, whereas adding intranasal corticosteroids to oral antihistamines outperforms doubling the antihistamine dose. Sola-Martínez and Zubiaga-Fernandez et al. report that exhaled decane and nonadecane may serve as non-invasive biomarkers distinguishing allergic from non-allergic individuals among patients with chronic rhinitis. Cardoso et al. show in a randomised, placebo-controlled trial that eight week supplementation with a heat-treated Bifidobacterium longum CECT 7347 postbiotic significantly reduced combined symptom and medication scores in adults with allergic rhinitis. Campion et al. show that out-of-season high-dose nasal birch pollen challenge raises allergen-specific IgE and effector cell sensitivity, while later attenuating the seasonal amplification of allergic responses in birch pollen-allergic adults. Leily et al. demonstrate that in the Isle of Wight birth cohort persistent Alternaria sensitisation from childhood to adulthood correlates with persistent asthma and, more strongly, rhinitis. Virkkula et al. report in a randomised controlled trial that full and limited endoscopic sinus surgery both improve quality of life in chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps, without a significant difference between the two approaches at 24 months. Bärhold et al. show that simultaneous dual type 2 biologic therapy improves sinonasal outcomes in selected patients with severe uncontrolled chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps and type 2 comorbidities. Dramburg and Hernandez Toro et al. use prospective e-Diary data from the @IT.2020 project to classify seasonal allergic rhinitis into mild, moderate, and severe clusters, revealing substantial recall bias in the retrospective ARIA classification. Sousa-Pinto et al. use MASK-air app data to show that both as-needed and regular medication use in the pollen season can achieve good symptom control and treatment satisfaction in allergic rhinitis. Hasegawa et al. link complement activation to fibrin deposition through complement-eosinophil crosstalk in eosinophilic chronic rhinosinusitis. Bousquet et al. discuss the need to assess on-demand versus continuous treatment in allergic rhinitis in the ARIA-EAACI guidelines. Han et al. report that increased cell adhesion molecule 5 expression in nasal polyps is associated with plasma cell infiltration.
